In what year was Catherine of Aragon born?
Catherine of Aragon: Catherine was born at the Archbishop's Palace of Alcalá de Henares, and was the youngest child of Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon.

Mitch McConnell: McConnell is in his seventh Senate term and is the longest-serving senator in Kentucky history.

Christopher Columbus: The name Christopher Columbus is the anglicization of the Latin Christophorus Columbus.

Yitzhak Rabin: Rabin was born in Jerusalem to Jewish immigrants from Eastern Europe and was raised in a Labor Zionist household.

Nelson Mandela: Mandela was born into the Thembu royal family in Mvezo, South Africa.

Law and Justice (Polish: Prawo i Sprawiedliwość, PiS) is a right-wing populist and national-conservative political party in Poland.

Carolingian Empire: The Carolingian Empire (800–887) was a Frankish-dominated empire in Western and Central Europe during the Early Middle Ages.

Sanseitō: Japan. It is on the far-right of the political spectrum.
In which country did the Battle on the Ice take place?
Battle on the Ice: Russia. The Battle on the Ice, also known as the Battle of Lake Peipus, took place on 5 April 1242.
In which country was Falange Española based?
Falange Española: Spain. Falange Española (FE) was a Spanish fascist and national syndicalist political organization active from 1933 to 1934.
In which country is Heian period?
Heian period: Japan. The Heian period (平安時代, Heian jidai) is the last division of classical Japanese history, running from 794 to 1185.
In which country is Socialism with Chinese characteristics based?

Socialism with Chinese characteristics: People's Republic of China. In the party's official narrative, socialism with Chinese characteristics is Marxism adapted to Chinese conditions and a product of scientific socialism.
In which country is History of Massachusetts?

History of Massachusetts: United States. The area that is now Massachusetts was colonized by English settlers in the early 17th century and became the Commonwealth of Massachusetts in the 18th century.
In which country is Battle of Passchendaele?
Battle of Passchendaele: Belgium. Passchendaele (now Passendale) lies on the last ridge east of Ypres, 5 mi (8 km) from Roulers (now Roeselare), a junction of the Bruges-(Brugge)-to-Kortrijk railway.
In which country was the French Second Republic?
French Second Republic: France. The republic existed from 1848, when the monarchy fell, until its dissolution only four years later in 1852 upon the proclamation of the Second French Empire.
In which country was Han dynasty?
Han dynasty: Chinese Empire. It was succeeded by the Three Kingdoms period (220–280 AD) and also briefly interrupted by the Xin dynasty (9–23 AD) established by the usurping regent Wang Mang.
In which country is Liberal Democrats based?
Liberal Democrats (UK): United Kingdom. The Liberal Democrats, colloquially known as the Lib Dems, is a political party in the United Kingdom.
Which of these is an official language of Ahmadiyya?
Ahmadiyya: Urdu. Adherents of the Ahmadiyya—a term adopted expressly in reference to Muhammad's alternative name Ahmad—are known as Ahmadi Muslims or simply Ahmadis.
Which of these was an official language of Goryeo?
Goryeo: Korean. Throughout its existence, Goryeo, alongside Unified Silla, was known to be the Golden Age of Buddhism in Korea.
Which of these was an official language of the Sasanian Empire?
Sasanian Empire: Middle Persian. It also helped shape European and Asian medieval art.
Which country uses the Reichsmark as its official currency?
The Reichsmark is the official currency of Nazi Germany. After Hitler was appointed Chancellor of Germany in 1933, the Nazi Party began to eliminate political opposition and consolidate power.

The son of an Irish mother and an Italian Civil War veteran, this Lower East Side native served four terms as New York's governor before becoming his party's 1928 presidential nominee — losing in a landslide to Herbert Hoover. Who was he?
Al Smith (December 30, 1873 - October 4, 1944) was an American politician who served as the 42nd governor of New York from 1919 to 1920 and again from 1923 to 1928.

This political theory leans heavily on the "non-aggression principle" to argue that even policing, courts, and defense could be supplied by private providers in a wholly voluntary society. What's this stateless ideology called?

Anarcho-capitalism (colloquially: ANCAP, Ancap, AnCap, or An-Cap) is a political ideology and economic theory that advocates for the abolition of state monopolies and promotes their replacement with private providers.

Convicted as a war criminal for his role in the deportation of Dutch Jews while serving as Reichskommissar of the Netherlands, this man had briefly been Austria's chancellor before the 1938 Anschluss — who was he?

Arthur Seyss-Inquart (Austrian German; 22 July 1892 - 16 October 1946) was an Austrian Nazi politician and convicted war criminal who served as Chancellor of Austria in 1938 for two days before the Anschluss.

Fought on September 19, 1356, during the Hundred Years' War, this clash saw Edward the Black Prince and 6,000 Anglo-Gascons defend a fortified position against 14,000 to 16,000 French attackers. Name it.
Battle of Poitiers was fought on 19 September 1356, during the Hundred Years' War, between a French army commanded by King John II and an Anglo-Gascon force under Edward, the Black Prince.
Born in the Quebec city of Baie-Comeau and once a prominent labour lawyer, he led the Progressive Conservatives to become Canada's 18th prime minister in 1984 — who was he?
Brian Mulroney (March 20, 1939 - February 29, 2024) was a Canadian lawyer, businessman, and politician who served as the 18th prime minister of Canada from 1984 to 1993.

The U.S. Navy's leading submarine authority, this fleet admiral commanded Allied forces across the Pacific during World War II and later helped win approval to build the first nuclear-powered submarine — who is he?
Chester W. Nimitz (24 February 1885 - 20 February 1966) was a fleet admiral in the United States Navy.
This American politician served as the 44th vice president under George H. W. Bush, after representing Indiana in both houses of Congress — who is he?

Dan Quayle (born February 4, 1947) is an American retired politician and Indiana National Guard veteran who served as the 44th vice president of the United States from 1989 to 1993 under President George H. W. Bush.

A retired U.S. Army colonel who led an early tank battle in the Gulf War and helped plan the 1999 NATO bombing of Yugoslavia, this officer later wrote a 1997 book arguing for radical Army reform. Who is he?
Douglas Macgregor (born January 4, 1947) is a retired colonel in the United States Army, former government official, author, consultant, and political commentator.
Closely aligned with Joseph Stalin's Soviet Union, this German communist leader died in 1944 after leading his party's opposition to the Weimar Republic in its final years — who is he?
Ernst Thälmann (16 April 1886 - 18 August 1944) was a German communist politician, revolutionary, and leader of the Communist Party of Germany (KPD) from 1925 to 1933.
He began on the Catholic nationalist right and served under Vichy before moving left to become the first left-wing president of France's Fifth Republic — and its longest-serving. Who was he?
François Mitterrand (26 October 1916 - 8 January 1996) was President of France from 1981 to 1995.

In November 1688 the Catholic King James II was deposed in favor of his daughter Mary II and her Dutch husband William of Orange — an event some historians call the last successful invasion of England. What is it called?

Glorious Revolution was the deposition of King James II in November 1688. The two ruled as joint monarchs of England, Scotland, and Ireland until Mary's death in 1694, when William became ruler in his own right.

Commissioned into a light horse unit his own father raised, he became the first Australian to reach lieutenant general and led the Desert Mounted Corps to one of military history's fastest pursuits. Who was this WWI commander?

Harry Chauvel (16 April 1865 - 4 March 1945) was a senior officer of the Australian Imperial Force who fought at Gallipoli and during the Sinai and Palestine Campaign in the Middle Eastern theatre of the First World War.
Formed in 1942 from earlier Polish resistance cells, this underground force became one of WWII Europe's largest, fighting German occupiers under London-exiled leadership — which organization?
Home Army (abbreviated AK) was the dominant resistance movement in German-occupied Poland during World War II.
The son of Abraham and Sarah and father of Jacob and Esau, this patriarch's name means 'he will laugh,' referencing his parents' reaction to news of his birth at their advanced ages — who is he?
Isaac is the second Hebrew patriarch in Judaism and an important figure in the Abrahamic religions, including Samaritanism, Christianity, Islam, the Bah' Faith, and Rastafari.
Whose decades campaigning on immigration and "traditional values" so shifted French debate that it spawned a coined term for the "-isation of minds" — the founder of the National Front?
Jean-Marie Le Pen (20 June 1928 - 7 January 2025) was a French politician who founded the far-right National Front (now National Rally) party.

Starting in 1950 this Wisconsin senator became the public face of Cold War fears, alleging communists had infiltrated the government, universities, and Hollywood — until the Senate censured him in 1954. Who was he?
Joseph McCarthy (November 14, 1908 - May 2, 1957) was an American politician who served as a Republican senator from Wisconsin from 1947 until his death in 1957.
Representing a Berlin district in the Bundestag, this politician chaired the SPD's youth organization before rising to General Secretary of the party — who is he?
Kevin Kühnert (born 1 July 1989) is a German politician of Social Democratic Party (SPD) who served as member of the Bundestag from 2021 to 2025, representing Berlin-Tempelhof-Schneberg.
Fueled in part by the country's religious mosaic of Christians, Sunnis, Shias, and Druze, which 1975–1990 conflict killed an estimated 150,000 and drove nearly a million people into exile?
Lebanese Civil War was a multifaceted armed conflict that took place from 1975 to 1990.
He served as Senegal's prime minister from 2004 to 2007 before a falling-out with his mentor led him to found a new party and later win the presidency in 2012 — who is he?
Macky Sall (French; born 11 December 1961) is a Senegalese politician who served as the fourth president of Senegal from 2012 to 2024.
In a memorable episode, this Pakistani chief minister's own Wikipedia page was cited by the Attorney General as proof of her academic credentials — who is she?
Maryam Nawaz (born 28 October 1973) is a Pakistani politician who has served as the 19th chief minister of Punjab since 26 February 2024.
A 1991 graduate of an elite airborne academy, this Ukrainian-born officer has led Russia's paratrooper forces since 2022 - who is he?
Mikhail Teplinsky (born 9 January 1969) is a Ukrainian-born Russian military officer who has served as commander of the Russian Airborne Forces since 2022.
The 126th holder of his throne and a one-time history student at Oxford, he became emperor in 2019 when his father Akihito abdicated — who is he?
Naruhito (born 23 February 1960) is Emperor of Japan.

Known as the 'Demon Daimyo,' this Japanese samurai and warlord is regarded as the first 'Great Unifier' of Japan during the Sengoku period, alongside retainers Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu — who is he?
Oda Nobunaga (23 June 1534 - 21 June 1582) was a Japanese samurai and daimy and one of the leading figures of the Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama periods.
A silversmith from Boston's North End, this American rode at midnight in 1775 to warn militia of British troops marching toward Lexington and Concord. Who is this?
Paul Revere was American silversmith and military officer (1735–1818).
Suspended in a soybean-oil and lecithin emulsion that gives it a milky white color, this intravenous anesthetic is prized for quick recovery — what is it?
Propofol is the active component of an intravenous anesthetic used for induction and maintenance of general anesthesia.
A former Navy veteran and healthcare executive, he served two terms as Florida's governor before becoming the state's senior U.S. senator in 2019 — who is he?
Rick Scott (n Myers; born December 1, 1952) is an American attorney, businessman, politician, and Navy veteran serving as the senior United States senator from Florida, a seat he has held since 2019.
As students in 1930s Paris, he and Michel Aflaq blended nationalism and socialism into a doctrine, then co-founded the Ba'ath Party — and he was later assassinated in Paris in 1980. Who was he?
Salah al-Din al-Bitar (1 January 1912 - 21 July 1980) was a Syrian politician who co-founded the Baath Party with Michel Aflaq in the early 1940s.
After a 2022 split in a Maharashtra party, this faction led by former chief minister Uddhav Thackeray received a new 'Flaming Torch' symbol from India's Election Commission — which faction?
Shiv Sena (UBT) (Uddhav Balasaheb Thackeray) is a Hindutva-based, Marathi regionalist, nationalist political party formed in 2022.
Now leading an alternate government from exile in Lithuania and Poland, this Belarusian opposition figure stepped into the 2020 presidential race after her husband's arrest — who is she?
Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya (ne Pilipchuk; born 11 September 1982) is a Belarusian opposition leader and political activist.

This Japanese term describes marginalized, sometimes homeless young people who gather in the alleys around Tokyo's Shinjuku Toho Building — many of them runaways seeking a sense of community after experiencing bullying — what's the term?
Toyoko kids is a Japanese term describing marginalized youth, including some homeless, who gather in the back alleys around the Shinjuku Toho Building in Kabukicho.
This Russian right-wing populist politician led a nationalist party from its 1992 founding until his death in 2022, twice serving as deputy chairman of the State Duma. Who is he?

Vladimir Zhirinovsky (25 April 1946 - 6 April 2022) was a Russian right-wing populist politician who served as the leader of the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR) from its creation in 1992 until his death in 2022.

This 2023 musical fantasy directed by Paul King stars Timothée Chalamet and serves as a prequel to the 1971 film, portraying the protagonist's early days as a chocolatier. What is this film adaptation based on Roald Dahl's novel called?
Wonka (film) is a 2023 musical fantasy film directed by Paul King, who co-wrote the screenplay with Simon Farnaby.

Sparked by the assassination of India's prime minister at the hands of her own bodyguards, this wave of organized violence killed thousands nationwide after a military raid on a Punjab temple complex — what was it?
1984 anti-Sikh riots: Series of organised pogroms in India.

This sweeping historical period saw two new superpowers emerge, the United Nations get founded, Western Europe rebuilt under the Marshall Plan, and colonies across Asia and Africa gain independence — what period is this?
Aftermath of World War II: Events after the end of the war in 1945.
Once Vladimir Putin's chief bodyguard, this Russian official oversaw the 2014 annexation of Crimea before serving as Governor of Tula Oblast?
Aleksey Dyumin: Russian lieutenant general and politician (born 1972)

Amon Göth: Austrian military officer and war criminal (1908–1946)
Founder of the German Workers' Party that became the Nazi Party, this early mentor to Adolf Hitler was ousted from party leadership by his protégé in 1921 — who is he?
Chile's longest-serving head of state seized power in a 1973 coup against Salvador Allende and ruled until 1990, leaving thousands of opponents tortured or killed — who was he?
Augusto Pinochet: Dictator of Chile from 1973 to 1990.
Fought in Somalia's capital on 3-4 October 1993 and later dramatized as 'Black Hawk Down,' this clash pitted U.S. forces against Somali National Alliance fighters loyal to General Aidid?
Battle of Mogadishu (1993): Military conflict during the Somali Civil War.
Born Warren Wilhelm Jr., this Democratic politician served as New York City's public advocate before becoming its 110th mayor and describing economic inequality as a 'tale of two cities' — who is he?
Bill de Blasio: Mayor of New York City from 2014 to 2021.
As Adam and Eve's firstborn, this farmer grew jealous when God favored his brother's offering over his own, leading to history's first fratricide — who was he?
Dubbed the 'Champion of Farmers' for his land reform work, this Indian independence activist briefly served as prime minister from July 1979 to January 1980 — who is he?
Charan Singh: Prime Minister of India from 1979 to 1980. Singh was principally known for his land and agricultural reform initiatives, and was Member of Parliament (MP) for Baghpat.
Considered by some the greatest lawyer of the 20th century, this ACLU leader argued the Leopold and Loeb case and the Scopes 'monkey' trial — who is he?
Clarence Darrow: American lawyer and politician (1857–1938)
Rising from Persis to topple the Median Empire, this ruler founded the Achaemenid dynasty and built what became, in its day, the largest empire the world had yet seen — who was he?
Cyrus the Great: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire. Cyrus II of Persia (c. 600 – 530 BC), commonly known as Cyrus the Great, was the founder of the Achaemenid Empire.
Dubbed the "Architect of Modern China," this Sichuan-born leader steered the nation toward a socialist market economy after Mao's death — who was he?
Deng Xiaoping: Leader of China from 1978 to 1989.

Before leading the commission that investigated the 1963 Kennedy assassination, which California governor became chief justice and authored the majority opinions in Brown v. Board of Education and Miranda v. Arizona?
Earl Warren: Chief Justice of the United States from 1953 to 1969.
Elected as a moderate Republican in 2014, this New York congresswoman later chaired the House Republican Conference and grilled university presidents in a viral 2023 hearing — who is she?
Born into rural poverty, she moved to Buenos Aires at 15 to chase acting before becoming Argentina's beloved First Lady — affectionately called 'Evita,' who was she?
Eva Perón: First Lady of Argentina from 1946 to 1952.
Fought mainly for influence over Korea and ending with the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895, this conflict pitted the Qing dynasty against the Empire of Japan — what was this conflict called?
First Sino-Japanese War: 1894–1895 war between China and Japan.
The first female student at Abeokuta Grammar School, this Nigerian educator and women's-rights organizer wove together anti-imperialist, Pan-Africanist, and feminist ideals — who is she?
The eldest son of former Indonesian president Joko Widodo, this politician became vice president in 2024 as running mate to Prabowo Subianto after serving as mayor of Surakarta — who is he?
Gibran Rakabuming Raka: Vice President of Indonesia since 2024.
After his father was executed in the Stockholm Bloodbath, he led a war of liberation and was elected king in 1523 — the day Sweden left the Kalmar Union and now its National Day. Which Swedish king?
Gustav Vasa: King of Sweden from 1523 to 1560.
He was Iran's top negotiator with the EU three before becoming the country's seventh president in 2013 — which sharia-lawyer-turned-cleric served until 2021?
Hassan Rouhani: President of Iran from 2013 to 2021. Hassan Rouhani (born Hassan Fereydoun, 12 November 1948) is an Iranian politician who served as the seventh president of Iran from 2013 to 2021.
Spanning roughly 1000 to 1300 CE, this European era saw a population boom, the 12th-century renaissance, and the growth of cities before the Black Death struck — which period?
High Middle Ages: Period of European history between AD 1000 and 1350.

It runs from our species' emergence in Africa some 300,000 years ago, through the great migration out during the last Ice Age, to the Neolithic farms and earliest writing systems — what sweeping subject is this?
Human history: Records of Earth's people.
A conflict from 1922 to 1923 following Irish independence, fought between the Provisional Government of Ireland and the Anti-Treaty IRA over the Anglo-Irish Treaty. What is this?

Irish Civil War: 1922–1923 conflict between factions of the IRA. The National Army benefited from substantial quantities of weapons provided by the British government, particularly artillery and armoured cars.
The only sitting member of the U.S. House ever elected president, this 20th commander-in-chief died in 1881 after being shot just months into office — who is he?
James A. Garfield: President of the United States in 1881.
A protégé of Martin Luther King Jr., this Baptist minister and civil rights leader founded the organizations that merged into the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition — who is he?
Jesse Jackson: American minister, activist and politician (1941–2026)
One of the richest men of his era, this fourth son of Edward III took his name from the Flemish city of his birth and founded the royal House of Lancaster; who was he?
John of Gaunt: English prince and regent (1340–1399)
Roman emperor from 527 to 565, his dream of restoring the empire saw his general Belisarius reclaim North Africa, Italy and Rome from the Ostrogoths — who was he?
Justinian I: Roman emperor from 527 to 565. The praetorian prefect Liberius reclaimed the south of the Iberian Peninsula, establishing the province of Spania.
This 7th-century Arab horseman first fought against Muhammad for the Quraysh, then converted and led Muslim armies through Iraq and Syria — who was he?
Khalid ibn al-Walid: Arab Muslim general (died 642)
Assassinated by the SS during the Night of the Long Knives in 1934, this German officer had served as the second-to-last chancellor of the Weimar Republic — who was he?
Kurt von Schleicher: Chancellor of Germany from 1932 to 1933.

A former aide to Herbert Hoover turned investment banker, he became an original member and later chairman of the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission and a major figure in postwar nuclear policy — who was he?
He quit school after second grade, didn't read until age ten, and went from metalworker and union firebrand to president of Brazil — who is it?
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva: President of Brazil (2003–2011; since 2023)
A sepoy in the Bengal Native Infantry who died in April 1857, this soldier's actions helped spark the rebellion that ended East India Company rule and ushered in the British Raj — who is he?
Mangal Pandey: Indian soldier and freedom fighter (1827–1857)
Imprisoned by Israel since 2002 on charges tied to deadly attacks he denies involvement in, this Palestinian legislator has long championed a two-state solution — who is he?
Married to the heir apparent of a Scandinavian throne, this royal underwent a lung transplant in 2026 after a diagnosis of pulmonary fibrosis — who is she?
Princess Beatrice of the United Kingdom
Mette-Marit, Crown Princess of Norway: Norwegian royal (born 1973)

Historians generally date this current period of human history from around 1500, though many now reserve its label for events from the 19th century onward, like the Industrial Revolution — what span of time is this?
Modern era: Current period of history. Since the 1990s, it has been more common among historians to refer to the period after the Middle Ages and up to the 19th century as the early modern period.
Son of Mehmed III and Halime Sultan, this Ottoman ruler held the throne twice, briefly in 1617–1618 and again in 1622–1623 — who was he?
Mustafa I: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire (r. 1617–1618, 1622–1623)
Widely seen as ill-prepared to rule a vast empire, he was the last monarch to reign before the Russian Revolution and led his country into World War I — which emperor?
Nicholas II: Emperor of Russia from 1894 to 1917.
This four-star general commanded the defense of Kyiv and led the 2022 Kharkiv counteroffensive before becoming commander-in-chief of Ukraine's armed forces in 2024 — who is he?
This historical region of northeastern Greater Iran became the political and cultural base of the Parni people and the Arsacid dynasty — lending its name to a famous empire. Which region?

Parthia: Historical region located in northeastern Iran. Parthia (Old Persian: 𐎱𐎼𐎰𐎺 Parθava; Parthian: 𐭐𐭓𐭕𐭅 Parθaw; Middle Persian: 𐭯𐭫𐭮𐭥𐭡𐭥 Pahlaw) is a historical region located in northeastern Greater Iran.

Its name comes from Ancient Greek for "love of wisdom," and once upon a time physics and psychology were considered branches of it before going their separate academic ways. What rational, critical field is this?
Philosophy: Study of general and fundamental questions.
This Macedonian Greek general, one of Alexander the Great's most trusted companions, retrieved his leader's body after his death and founded a new ruling dynasty in Egypt — who is he?
Ptolemy I Soter: Pharaoh of Egypt from 305 to 282 BC.
This Cuban revolutionary succeeded his brother as president in 2008 and served as the country's defense minister for nearly five decades — who is he?
Raúl Castro: President of Cuba from 2008 to 2018.
Abrasive and reactionary, this right-wing populist and economic nationalist served as New Zealand's 31st prime minister from 1975 to 1984 — who was he?
Robert Muldoon: Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1975 to 1984. After a troubled childhood, Muldoon served as a corporal and sergeant in the army in the Second World War.

On a single 1929 day in a Chicago garage, seven men were lined against a wall and gunned down — some of the killers disguised as police — in a brutal flashpoint of Prohibition-era gang warfare. What is this killing known as?

Saint Valentine's Day Massacre: 1929 gang shooting in Chicago. The Saint Valentine's Day Massacre was the murder of seven members and associates of Chicago's North Side Gang on Saint Valentine's Day 1929.

This wave of mass production, standardization, and rapid scientific discovery, sometimes dubbed the Technological era, is generally dated between 1870 and the outbreak of World War I in 1914. What period was this?
Second Industrial Revolution: 1870–1914 electrical and chemical era.
A writer who governed Tokyo from 1999 to 2012, this prominent ultranationalist was widely criticized for xenophobic and racist remarks against Chinese and Koreans in Japan — who was he?
Across religions this immortal, immaterial essence goes by many names — atman in Hinduism, jiva in Jainism, ruh in Islam — but what's its common English term?
Soul: In religion and philosophy, immaterial essence of a living being.
A London School of Economics graduate from a wealthy family, he led Togo from its 1958 election to independence as prime minister and then president, until his 1963 assassination — who was he?

Sylvanus Olympio: President of Togo from 1960 to 1963. After World War II, Olympio became prominent in efforts for independence of Togo and his party won the 1958 election, making him the prime minister of the country.
Founded by Aleister Crowley in the early 1900s, this occult philosophy centers on discovering one's 'True Will' and the maxim 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law' — what is it?
Thelema: New religious movement founded by Aleister Crowley.
This Haitian general rose from a slave rebellion to become Governor-General-for-life of Saint-Domingue before ultimately clashing with Napoleon's troops. Who was he?
Toussaint Louverture: Haitian general and revolutionary (1744–1803)
Composed in an archaic Sanskrit dialect, this collection of four ancient hymn texts forms the oldest layer of Hindu scripture — what are they collectively called?
This Warring States-era Chinese general commanded conquests of three rival kingdoms and is remembered by tradition as one of the four greatest generals of the late Warring States period — who was he?
Wang Jian (Qin): 3rd century BC Chinese military general.
Known as "Bill," this British field marshal led the so-called "forgotten army" in the Burma campaign before later serving as governor-general of Australia — who was he?
William Slim, 1st Viscount Slim: British Army field marshal, Governor-General of Australia, and author (1891–1970)

This Israeli politician served as defense minister from 2022 until his dismissal by the prime minister in November 2024, having earlier held posts including construction, immigration, and education minister after starting out in the navy. Who is he?
Yoav Gallant: Israeli politician & military officer (born 1958)
Who wrote Universal Declaration of Human Rights?

Universal Declaration of Human Rights → United Nations General Assembly. All 193 member states of the UN have ratified at least one of the nine binding treaties influenced by the Declaration, with the vast majority ratifying four or more.
Which of these people was born first?
Thomas Carlyle (born 1795) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was born first?
Stephen Hales (born 1677) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four was founded earliest?
MATLAB (founded 1984) is the earliest of the four. MATLAB (Matrix Laboratory) is a proprietary multi-paradigm programming language and numeric computing environment developed by MathWorks.
Which of these is a physicist?
John Logie Baird is a physicist. In 1928, the Baird Television Development Company achieved the first transatlantic television transmission.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Ingrid Daubechies is a mathematician. Baroness Ingrid Daubechies ( doh-bə-SHEE; French: [dobʃi]; born 17 August 1954) is a Belgian-American physicist and mathematician at Duke University.
What is the atomic number of Darmstadtium?
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Ds and atomic number 110.
What is the atomic number of Gold?
Gold is a chemical element; its chemical symbol is Au (from Latin aurum) and atomic number 79.
In what year did Kitty Oppenheimer die?
Kitty Oppenheimer: Robert Oppenheimer, the director of the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos Laboratory during World War II.
In what year was Boron discovered?
Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.
Dopamine: Pfizer. Dopamine (DA, a contraction of 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine) is a neuromodulatory molecule that plays several important roles in cells.
In which country is TAI TF Kaan?
TAI TF Kaan: Turkey. Designed to replace the Turkish Air Force’s fleet of F-16 Fighting Falcons, the Kaan is also intended for export to international markets.
Who is credited with discovering Leo Minor?
Leo Minor: Johannes Hevelius. Leo Minor is a small and faint constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Graph theory?
Graph theory: Leonhard Euler. In mathematics and computer science, graph theory is the study of graphs, which are mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects.
Who is credited with discovering Budesonide?
Budesonide: Ralph Brattsand. Budesonide, sold under the brand name Pulmicort, among others, is a steroid medication.
Who is credited with discovering Platinum?
Platinum: Julius Caesar Scaliger. Platinum is a chemical element; it has symbol Pt and atomic number 78.
A broad-spectrum benzimidazole drug, this medicine clears intestinal parasites from pinworm to hookworm to tapeworm — which agent is it?
Albendazole is a broad-spectrum antihelmintic and antiprotozoal agent of the benzimidazole type.
Famed for foundational work in number theory and algebraic geometry, this French mathematician was also a principal founder of the secretive Bourbaki group — who was he?
André Weil (6 May 1906 - 6 August 1998) was a French mathematician, known for his foundational work in number theory and algebraic geometry.

In 2003, this American mountaineer amputated his own trapped forearm with a dull pocket knife after five days pinned by a boulder in a Utah canyon, then rappelled and hiked miles to safety — who is he?

Aron Ralston (born October 27, 1975) is an American mountaineer, mechanical engineer, and motivational speaker, known for surviving a canyoneering accident in 2003 by cutting off part of his own right arm.
The second-largest living rodents after capybaras, these large semiaquatic mammals of the Northern Hemisphere have webbed back feet, hand-like front paws, and flat, scaly tails — name the animal?
Beaver (genus Castor) are large semiaquatic rodents of the Northern Hemisphere.
Composed mostly of plasma along with red cells, white cells, and platelets, this body fluid ferries oxygen and nutrients to cells while hauling waste away — name the fluid?

Blood is a body fluid in the circulatory system of humans and other vertebrates that delivers necessary substances such as nutrients and oxygen to the cells of the body, and transports metabolic waste products away from those same cells.
The only living group in its tribe, this genus of over 250 fuzzy bees forms small colonies under a single queen — and unlike honeybees, its females can sting again and again — what is it?
Bumblebee (or bumble bee, bumble-bee, or humble-bee) is any of over 250 species in the genus Bombus, part of Apidae, one of the bee families.
Which Mediterranean evergreen tree, grown mainly in Spain, produces edible seed pods often ground into a chocolate substitute, with seeds that yield a gum used as a food thickener?
Carob (Ceratonia siliqua) is a flowering evergreen tree or shrub in the Caesalpinioideae subfamily of the legume family, Fabaceae.
The principal sterol of all animals, it concentrates in the brain and spinal cord and is essential to every cell membrane — yet too much in the blood spells trouble. What is it?
Cholesterol is the principal sterol of all animals, distributed in body tissues, especially the brain and spinal cord, and in animal fats and oils.

The most widely distributed corvid, this large all-black bird is found across the Northern Hemisphere and is the heaviest passerine bird, with 11 accepted subspecies showing little variation in appearance. What bird is this?
Common raven (Corvus corax) is a large all-black passerine bird.
Its name comes from the Greek for "dark blue," and its anion — a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen — is so toxic that salts like the sodium and potassium forms cause swift poisoning. What is it?
Cyanide (from Greek kyanos 'dark blue') is an inorganic chemical compound that contains a CN functional group.
Known from thousands of fossils pulled from the La Brea Tar Pits, this extinct species of canine roamed the Americas until about 10,000 years ago. Name the species?
Dire wolf (Aenocyon dirus) is an extinct species of canine which was native to the Americas during the Late Pleistocene and Early Holocene epochs (125,000-10,000 years ago).
This mammal family includes living species from two genera as well as extinct giants like the woolly mammoth, and was first scientifically described in 1821 — what family is it?

Elephantidae is a family of large, herbivorous proboscidean mammals which includes the living elephants (belonging to the genera Elephas and Loxodonta), as well as a number of extinct genera like Mammuthus (mammoths) and Palaeoloxodon.

Built by a consortium of Airbus, BAE Systems and Leonardo for four NATO nations, this twin-engine canard delta-wing fighter grew out of the 1983 Future European Fighter Aircraft programme — which jet?
Eurofighter Typhoon is a European multinational twin-engine, supersonic, canard delta wing, multirole fighter.

This genetic neurodevelopmental disorder causes a long, narrow face, large ears, and unusually flexible fingers, with males typically far more affected than females and average IQ under 55 in affected boys — what's the condition?

Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder. The average IQ in males with FXS is under 55, while affected females tend to be in the borderline to normal range, typically around 70–85.
The last living species in an order that first appeared over 290 million years ago, this disease-resistant "living fossil" with fan-shaped leaves is also called the maidenhair tree — which is it?
Ginkgo biloba (-goh), also known as the maidenhair tree, and often misspelled "gingko" (see Etymology below) is a species of gymnosperm tree native to East Asia.
This flatfish's English name blends words for 'holy' and 'flat fish,' a nod to its place on the Catholic holy-day menu. Which bottom-dwelling fish?
Halibut is the common name for three species of flatfish in the family of right-eye flounders.
Nesting monogamously in tree cavities across Africa, Asia, and Melanesia, these birds are unique for having their first two neck vertebrae fused solid — which birds?
Hornbill are birds found in tropical and subtropical Africa, Asia and Melanesia of the family Bucerotidae.

Co-creator of the breakthrough neural network AlexNet and a contributor to landmark AI systems including GPT and AlphaGo, this computer scientist has won a major deep-learning research award three years running — who is he?
Ilya Sutskever (born 1986) is a computer scientist who specializes in machine learning.
This German-American software engineer designed PayPal's real-time anti-fraud system, then co-founded a site whose very first video — "Me at the zoo" — he uploaded himself in April 2005. Who is he?
Jawed Karim (born October 28, 1979) is a German and American software engineer and internet entrepreneur.
This pain-relieving, fever-reducing drug belongs to the propionic acid class of anti-inflammatories and hit the market in 1980, thirteen years after being patented — what is it?
Ketoprofen is one of the propionic acid class of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) with analgesic and antipyretic effects.
This bacterial blood infection, spread between humans, dogs, and rodents, can range from symptomless to a severe form that turns skin and eyes yellow and shuts down the kidneys — what disease is it?
Leptospirosis is a blood infection caused by bacteria of the genus Leptospira that can infect humans, dogs, rodents, and many other wild and domesticated animals.
Born in Vienna into one of Europe's richest families, this philosopher studied under Bertrand Russell at Cambridge and transformed 20th-century philosophy of language and logic — who is he?

Ludwig Wittgenstein ((h)tyne; Austrian; 26 April 1889 - 29 April 1951) was an Austro-British philosopher who worked in logic, philosophy of mathematics, philosophy of mind, and philosophy of language.

In 1835 she and Caroline Herschel became the first female Honorary Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, and decades later this Scottish polymath's name topped John Stuart Mill's women's-suffrage petition. Who is she?
Mary Somerville (ne Fairfax, formerly Greig; 1780-1872) was a Scottish scientist, writer, and polymath.
Built primarily from stainless steel, this Soviet supersonic interceptor could exceed Mach 3.2, but doing so risked wrecking its own engines. What aircraft is it?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25 (NATO reporting name: Foxbat) is a supersonic interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft that is among the fastest military aircraft to enter service.
This genus of bacteria lacks a cell wall entirely, making it naturally immune to antibiotics like penicillin that target cell-wall synthesis — name this genus?
Mycoplasma is a genus of bacteria that, like the other members of the class Mollicutes, lack a cell wall (peptidoglycan) around their cell membrane.
A child prodigy turned MIT mathematician, this American thinker is considered the originator of cybernetics — the science of communication in living things and machines. Who was he?
Norbert Wiener (November 26, 1894 - March 18, 1964) was an American computer scientist, mathematician, and philosopher.
Often silent at first, this disease arises from an ovary or nearby structures and announces itself only later with bloating, pelvic pain, and abdominal swelling — what is it?
Ovarian cancer is a cancerous tumor of an ovary.
This flowering plant is the sole genus in its own botanical family and ranges from knee-high herbaceous perennials to woody shrubs over ten feet tall — what plant is it?
Peony is any flowering plant in the genus Paeonia, the only genus in the family Paeoniaceae.

This roundworm is one of the most common intestinal parasites in humans, causing a condition sometimes called oxyuriasis after the family it belongs to, and has also been found in bonnet macaques — what's the parasite?
Pinworm (parasite) (species Enterobius vermicularis), also known as threadworm (in the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand) or seatworm, is a parasitic worm.
Originating on Gran Canaria and Tenerife, this large Spanish mastiff-type breed was traditionally used to guard property, herd livestock, and, legally until 1936, fight other dogs — what breed is it?
Presa Canario is a Spanish breed of large dog of mastiff or catch dog type.
It can form not just from rain but from mist, spray, or dew, and though we usually see an arc, it can actually be a full circle — what optical phenomenon is it?
Rainbow is an optical phenomenon caused by refraction, internal reflection and dispersion of light in water droplets resulting in a continuous spectrum of light appearing in the sky.
Named for its type genus, this plant family of nearly 4,800 species includes the trees and shrubs behind apples, pears, plums, cherries, and peaches — what family is it?
Rosaceae is a family of flowering plants that includes 4,828 known species in 91 genera.

Seven living species make up this group of ocean-dwelling reptiles, five of which are threatened with extinction — one species, found only near Australia, Papua New Guinea, and Indonesia, is not — name this group?
Sea turtle (superfamily Chelonioidea), sometimes called marine turtles, are reptiles of the order Testudines and of the suborder Cryptodira.
Commonly but inaccurately nicknamed for a big cat it wasn't closely related to, this extinct genus of saber-toothed predator roamed the Americas until as recently as 8,200 years ago — which genus?
Smilodon is a genus of extinct felids. It is one of the best-known saber-toothed predators and prehistoric mammals.
A Canadian cognitive psychologist at Harvard who champions evolutionary psychology and the computational theory of mind, which popular-science author wrote on how children learn irregular verb forms?
Steven Pinker (born September 18, 1954) is a Canadian cognitive psychologist, psycholinguist, popular science author, and public intellectual.
Born in 1946, this American serial killer often posed as an authority figure or feigned injury to lure young women to his car before assaulting and murdering them — who was he?
Ted Bundy (n Cowell; November 24, 1946 - January 24, 1989) was an American serial killer who kidnapped, raped and murdered dozens of young women and girls throughout 1974, 1975, and 1978.
This metric unit of mass equals exactly 1,000 kilograms — about 2,204.6 pounds — and is technically identical to the SI unit called the megagram. What is it?
Tonne (or; symbol: t) is a unit of mass equal to 1,000 kilograms.
Native to Europe and southwestern Asia, this herbaceous perennial flowering plant is the type species of its genus and a member of the honeysuckle family — which herb?
Valerian (herb) (Valeriana officinalis) is an herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Caprifoliaceae, native to Europe and southwestern Asia.
Caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene, this inherited condition lets copper build up in the liver and brain, leading to tremors, personality changes, and yellowing skin — which condition?
Wilson's disease (also called hepatolenticular degeneration) is a genetic disorder characterized by the excess build-up of copper in the body.
Also known by his Latinized name Rhazes, this Persian polymath authored over 200 manuscripts on medicine, philosophy, and astronomy during the Islamic Golden Age — who was he?
Abu Bakr al-Razi: 10th-century Iranian physician and polymath.
Based on a civilian widebody jet, this European aerial-refueling tanker holds over 90% of the air-to-air refueling market outside the United States, with 17 countries as customers — which aircraft?

Airbus A330 MRTT: Aerial refuelling tanker aircraft. The Airbus A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT) is a European aerial refueling and military transport aircraft based on the civilian Airbus A330.
About one-third the density of steel, this soft, nonmagnetic, silver-looking metal grows a protective oxide skin the instant it meets air — which element, symbol Al?
Aluminium: Chemical element with atomic number 13 (Al)
Triggered by either histamine or bradykinin, this rapid swelling of the deep skin layers can affect the face, tongue, or airway within minutes — what is it?
Angioedema: Disease characterized by rapid swelling.

Once mistaken for bacteria, this domain of single-celled organisms is now known to be the group from which eukaryotes evolved, distinguished by ether-linked cell membranes and a unique whip-like motility structure. What domain is it?
Archaea: Domain of organisms. Traditionally, Archaea included only its prokaryotic members, but has since been found to be paraphyletic, as eukaryotes are known to have evolved from archaea.
Affecting roughly one in five people at some point and usually starting in childhood, this long-term itchy, red, cracked-skin condition is also simply called eczema — what's its formal name?
Atopic dermatitis: Long-term form of skin inflammation.
A blood-feeding parasite of the genus Cimex that usually bites at night, this insect leaves itchy welts but, reassuringly, isn't known to spread any infectious disease — what is it?
Bed bug: Type of insect that feeds on human blood.
Despite its name, only the soles of this tawny, spotted feline's paws are actually dark — and at just 35 to 52 centimetres long, it ranks as Africa's smallest wild feline species — what animal is it?
Black-footed cat: Small wild cat native to Southern Africa.
Rooted in prehistoric herbalism for identifying edible and medicinal species, this branch of biology studies roughly 410,000 species of land plants — what field of study?
Named from the Greek word for butter, this oily, foul-smelling compound with the formula CH3CH2CH2COOH is a key component of the mammalian gut. What is it?
Butyric acid: Chemical compound (CH3CH2CH2COOH). It is an oily, colorless liquid with an unpleasant odor.
These biomolecules often follow the tidy empirical formula (CH2O)n, and as polysaccharides like starch, glycogen, and cellulose they store energy and build structure — what family are they?
Carbohydrate: Organic compound that consists only of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
Consisting mainly of the brain and spinal cord — and, surprisingly, the retina too — this part of the body integrates information to coordinate an animal's activity — what is it?
Central nervous system: Brain and spinal cord. The rest of this article exclusively discusses the vertebrate central nervous system, which is radically distinct from all other animals.
Sold as Thorazine, this drug was the first of the typical antipsychotics — used to treat schizophrenia and, oddly, hiccups that won't quit. What is it?
Their 'lady' actually refers to the Virgin Mary, and their cheerful red-and-black warning colours tell predators they taste terrible — what is this 6,000-species family of small beetles?
Coccinellidae: Family of beetles. The more than 6,000 described species have a global distribution and are found in a variety of habitats.
First created near Darmstadt in 1996 and named for an astronomer on his 537th anniversary, this synthetic element (number 112) is so volatile it may even be a gas — which element?
Copernicium: Chemical element with atomic number 112 (Cn)
Caused by prolonged exposure to excess cortisol, this condition produces abdominal weight gain with thin limbs, a rounded red face, and reddish stretch marks — which condition is it?
Cushing's syndrome: Symptoms from excessive exposure to glucocorticoids such as cortisol.

Known mainly through DNA evidence rather than plentiful fossils, this extinct archaic human group ranged across Asia until about 32,000 years ago, and DNA analysis confirmed the Harbin skull belonged to it — what group is it?
Denisovan: Archaic human species from Asia.
In 1949, this NASA mathematician became the first African-American woman to supervise a team at Langley, later teaching herself and her staff the Fortran language — who is she?
Dorothy Vaughan: American human computer and computer programmer (1910–2008)
This group of 13 genetic connective tissue disorders causes loose joints and stretchy, velvety skin, with a classification last updated in 2017 — what condition is it?
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Group of genetic connective tissues disorders. The existing classification was last updated in 2017, when a number of rarer forms of EDS were added.
Despite never earning a university degree, this German-American psychoanalyst taught at Harvard, Berkeley, and Yale, and coined the term 'identity crisis' — who is he?
Erik Erikson: American psychoanalyst and essayist (1902–1994)

With a red face, a black-and-white head, and a bold yellow wing bar, this small finch native to the Palearctic often appears in Italian Renaissance paintings of the Madonna and Child. What bird is it?
European goldfinch: Species of bird. It has been introduced to other areas, including Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay and the United States.
Also known as the bodhi tree, this species is revered in four South Asian religions as the tree beneath which Buddha is said to have reached enlightenment — which species?
Ficus religiosa: Species of fig. Ficus religiosa or sacred fig is a species of fig native to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina that belongs to Moraceae, the fig or mulberry family.
Known online by the alias TiAMO, this Swede co-founded a notorious file-sharing site and stood trial for it in 2009, a saga captured in the documentary TPB AFK — who is he?
This mathematician founded set theory and proved that there are more real numbers than natural numbers, revealing an infinity of infinities — who is he?
Known online by the alias 'anakata,' this Swedish computer specialist co-founded a notorious BitTorrent site and later helped WikiLeaks with its 2010 release of a leaked military video — who is he?
Gottfrid Svartholm: Swedish computer specialist. Parts of an interview with Svartholm commenting on the May 2006 police raid of The Pirate Bay are featured in Good Copy Bad Copy and Steal This Film.
Nicknamed the slime eel, this jawless marine scavenger is the only living animal with a skull but no proper backbone — what is it?
Hagfish: Class of eel-shaped, slime-producing animal.

Famous for the ideas of "bounded rationality" and "satisficing," this remarkable scholar won both a Turing Award and a Nobel in Economics — bridging computer science, economics, and psychology. Who was he?
Herbert A. Simon: American academic and Nobel Laureate (1916–2001)

Found only in the Americas from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, these roughly 375 species pull off rapid, maneuverable flight thanks to an exceptional metabolism — and their males flaunt the widest plumage diversity of any bird — what are they?
Named from an Ancient Greek word for 'intestinal obstruction,' this medical condition disrupts the gut's normal propulsive movement, whether from lost peristalsis or a physical blockage — what is it?
Ileus: Disruption to the propulsive ability of the intestine.
A self-taught rocketeer and practicing occultist, this co-founder of both JPL and Aerojet invented the first castable composite rocket propellant before dying young in 1952. Who was he?
Court astronomer and advisor to Elizabeth I, this mathematician-occultist kept one of England's largest libraries and is credited with coining the term "British Empire" — who was he?
John Dee: English scientist and occultist (1527–1608/09)
Convicted in 1995 of fraud and illegally intercepting communications, this hacker served five years in prison before founding his own computer-security consulting firm — who is he?
This probability principle explains why a casino might lose money on a single spin of roulette but reliably earns a predictable percentage over many thousands of spins. What is it called?
Law of large numbers: Averages of repeated trials converge to the expected value.
Instrumental in the discovery of nuclear fission, this Austrian-Swedish physicist fled Nazi Germany in 1938 after losing her post under the Nuremberg Laws — who is she?

Fired by IBM in 1968 for revealing her intent to transition — an apology that took until 2020 — this computer scientist had already invented dynamic instruction handling behind modern out-of-order execution. Who was she?
Lynn Conway: American computer scientist and electrical engineer (1938–2024)

Originally hoping to become an engineer, this Italian physician became one of the first women to graduate from medical school in Italy and later devised an influential educational philosophy — who is she?
Maria Montessori: Italian physician and educator (1870–1952)
Comprising 18 to 24 species that hybridize freely where their ranges overlap, this genus of the mint family thrives in wet, moist soils worldwide — what is it?
Mentha: Genus of flowering plants in the family Lamiaceae.
NATO nicknames it 'Foxhound,' and at roughly 3,000 km/h it's the fastest operational combat aircraft known — which interceptor, a Soviet successor to the MiG-25, is it?
Mikoyan MiG-31: Interceptor aircraft. The MiG-31 is the fastest known operational combat aircraft, with a top speed around 3,000 km/h (1,600 knots).
Built with a slender segmented body and a long piercing-and-sucking proboscis, this family of 3,600 fly species diversified back in the Cretaceous — what are they?
Mosquito: Family of flies. The word mosquito (formed by mosca and diminutive -ito) is Spanish and Portuguese for little fly.

This branch of alternative medicine rests on vitalism and folk healing rather than evidence, and its grab-bag of 'natural' methods runs from the thoroughly discredited to certain accepted psychotherapies. What is it?
Naturopathy: Form of alternative medicine. The ethics of naturopathy have been called into question by medical professionals and its practice has been characterized as quackery.
Nicknamed the 'winter vomiting disease' and spread by the fecal-oral route, this is the most common cause of gastroenteritis — what is it?
Norovirus: Type of viruses that cause gastroenteritis.

Numbering 126 species, these are the largest order of marsupials in the Western Hemisphere — and only one of them, the Virginia variety, made it as far north as the United States and Canada. What animal is this?
Nicknamed the 'white rats' of its phylum for how often it's cultivated in classrooms and labs, this single-celled ciliate thrives in stagnant ponds — what is it?
This nerve-damage condition can be triggered by diabetes, vitamin B12 deficiency, or certain chemotherapy and antibiotic drugs, and may come on suddenly or creep in slowly — what is it?
Peripheral neuropathy: Nervous system disease affecting nerves beyond the brain and spinal cord.
This French physicist shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife, making them the first married couple to win a Nobel — who is he?
Pierre Curie: French physicist and chemist (1859–1906)
Also called quaking aspen for the way its leaves flutter in the slightest breeze, which poplar species is native to the Old World's cool temperate regions?
Nicknamed 'gold cap' and 'golden halo,' this is the world's best-known psilocybin-containing mushroom thanks to its wide distribution and how easily it's cultivated — which species?
Psilocybe cubensis: Species of fungus. It belongs to the fungus family Hymenogastraceae and was previously known as Stropharia cubensis.
Also known as steelhead in its sea-run form, this North American Pacific species shows off a vivid reddish stripe along its flank in breeding males — which fish?
Rainbow trout: Fresh-water species of fish.
His 'Essai Sur La Nature Du Commerce' was called the 'cradle of political economy'; this Irish-French banker made a fortune speculating in John Law's Mississippi Company — who is it?
Richard Cantillon: Irish-French economist and banker (c. 1680 – 1734)
This light Swedish single-engine supersonic fighter has a delta wing and canard configuration with fly-by-wire controls and is fully NATO interoperable — what is it?
Saab JAS 39 Gripen: Light single-engined multirole fighter aircraft from Sweden.
Distinguished from true seals by external ear flaps and the ability to walk on all fours, these marine mammals include a giant subspecies that can weigh up to 1,000 kilograms. What are they?
Sea lion: Subfamily of aquatic mammals.

Composed of repeating siloxane units with a backbone of oxygen and silicon rather than carbon, this synthetic material fills sealants, cookware, and medical devices, and is often confused with the chip-making element it's named after — what is it?
Native to the Andes, this is the only living species in South America from the short-faced lineage, and unlike most of its relatives, eats mostly plants — which animal?
Spectacled bear: Species of mammal. The spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus), also known as the Andean bear, is a species of bear native to the Andes Mountains in northern and western South America.

Named after a Scottish village where it was discovered in 1790, this alkaline earth metal was first isolated in 1808 by Humphry Davy using electrolysis, and identified a year after its discovery by its crimson-red flame test. What element is it?
Strontium: Chemical element with atomic number 38 (Sr)
Known by folk names like bitter buttons and golden buttons, this Eurasian flowering plant in the daisy family has become invasive after being introduced to Australia and the Americas — which plant?
Tansy: Species of plant. Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare) is a perennial, herbaceous flowering plant in the genus Tanacetum in the family Asteraceae, native to temperate Europe and Asia.
This body region between the hip and the knee contains a single bone — the femur — that forms a ball-and-socket joint above and a hinge joint below. What is it?
Thigh: Body part between pelvis and knee; upper leg.
Caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii and often spread through undercooked meat or infected cat feces, this disease is famously dangerous to catch during pregnancy — what is it?
Normally containing two arteries and one vein cushioned in Wharton's jelly, this conduit links a developing fetus to the placenta — what is it?
Umbilical cord: Conduit between embryo/fetus and the placenta.

Most animals make their own, but humans, guinea pigs, and some bats must eat it because a synthesis-enzyme gene is broken; this citrus nutrient builds collagen and acts as an antioxidant — what is it?
Vitamin C: Essential nutrient found in citrus fruits and other foods.
Ranging from a few meters for Bluetooth to millions of kilometers for deep-space signals, this method of sending information relies on radio waves instead of cables -- what is it called?
Wireless: Transfer of information or power that does not require the use of physical wires.
Tellurium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for tellurium is Te. Tellurium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Te and atomic number 52.
Darmstadtium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for darmstadtium is Ds. Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Ds and atomic number 110.

In what year was Kiefer Sutherland born?
Kiefer Sutherland: Kiefer William Frederick Dempsey George Rufus Sutherland (born 21 December 1966) is a British and Canadian actor.
In what year was Gene Hackman born?
Gene Hackman: Eugene Allen Hackman (January 30, 1930 – February 18, 2025) was an American actor.
In what year was Maggie Smith born?
Maggie Smith: Dame Margaret Natalie Smith (28 December 1934 – 27 September 2024) was a British actress.
In what year was Alexis Bledel born?
Alexis Bledel: Kimberly Alexis Bledel ( blə-DEL; born September 16, 1981) is an American actress and model.
In what year was Seth Rogen born?
Seth Rogen: Seth Aaron Rogen ( ROH-gən; born April 15, 1982) is a Canadian actor, comedian, filmmaker, and cannabis entrepreneur.
In what year was Emilia Clarke born?
